questions.question: Which statement best describes a singularity of a function $f$ at $x_0$?
options: $f$ is continuous at $x_0$ but discontinuous at every nearby point.
$f$ fails at $x_0$ but is regular in a punctured neighbourhood.
$f$ is differentiable at $x_0$ but not continuous nearby.
$f$ is undefined on every interval containing $x_0$.

questions.question: Why is a punctured neighbourhood used when identifying a singularity at $x_0$?
options: It requires $f$ to be undefined at every point near $x_0$.
It checks that $f$ is well behaved near $x_0$ except possibly at $x_0$ itself.
It replaces the need to know whether $f$ is continuous at $x_0$.
It means that $x_0$ must be an endpoint of the domain.

questions.question: For $f(x)=\frac{1}{x}$, at which point does the singularity occur?
For $f(x) = \dfrac{x^2-1}{x-1}$, which point is a removable singularity?
Which situation rules out calling $x_0$ a singularity under the given definition?
options: $f$ is undefined at $x_0$ but continuous for nearby $x\ \neq x_0$.
$f$ is defined and continuous at $x_0$ and also near $x_0$.
$f$ is defined at $x_0$ but not continuous there, and is continuous nearby.
$f$ fails to behave regularly at $x_0$ but is regular arbitrarily close to it.

questions.question: Which feature is common to the singularities listed?
options: They all force the function values to become infinite.
They all occur only at endpoints of domains.
They mark failure of definition or continuity at one point.
They all make the function discontinuous at every nearby point.

questions.question: Suppose $f$ is defined and continuous for all $x$ in $(2-\delta,2)\cup(2,2+\delta)$, but $f$ is not defined at $x = 2$. What can be concluded from the definition?
options: $x = 2$ cannot be a singularity because $f$ is regular nearby.
$x = 2$ is a singularity of $f$.
$f$ must be continuous at $x = 2$.
$f$ has no punctured neighbourhood around $2$.

questions.question: Suppose $f$ is defined near $x_0$, is continuous for nearby $x\ \neq x_0$, but is not continuous at $x_0$. Which conclusion matches the definition?
options: $x_0$ is not a singularity because $f(x_0)$ exists.
$f$ has no irregular behaviour at $x_0$.
$f$ must be undefined on a punctured neighbourhood of $x_0$.
$x_0$ is a singularity of $f$.

questions.question: Why is the punctured-neighbourhood condition important for a singularity?
options: It proves that every discontinuity is removable.
It makes continuity at $x_0$ irrelevant to the definition.
It requires the function to be bounded near $x_0$.
It isolates an irregularity at $x_0$ from widespread nearby issues.

questions.question: Which statement correctly avoids overinterpreting singularity?
options: A singularity always means $\lim_{x\to x_0} f(x) = \infty$.
A singularity always disappears after redefining $f(x_0)$.
A singularity need not be infinite; it may be removable or essential.
A singularity can occur only when $f$ is not defined anywhere near $x_0$.

questions.question: Let $f(x) = \sin(\frac{1}{x})$., which point is an essential singularity?
options: $x = \pi$

questions.question: A function is continuous on $(a-\delta,a)\cup(a,a+\delta)$ and has a failure of definition at $a$. How should $a$ be classified using only the definition?
options: $a$ is automatically a removable discontinuity.
$a$ is automatically an essential singularity.
$a$ cannot be a singularity because continuity nearby is present.
$a$ is a singularity, but its type needs additional information.

questions.question: What kind of failure can make $x_0$ a singularity of $f$?
options: Failure of definition or continuity at $x_0$.
Failure of being increasing everywhere.
Failure of having a global maximum.
Failure of being a polynomial.

questions.question: What must happen near, but not at, a singularity?
options: The function is undefined at every nearby point.
The function must tend to infinity there.
The function is defined nearby, just not at the point itself.
The function must have a maximum.

questions.question: Which description best captures a singularity?
options: A point where every nearby value is undefined.
A point where the function must equal zero.
An isolated point of irregular behaviour.
A point where the graph must have a horizontal tangent.

questions.question: For $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{x-2}$, which point is the natural singularity?
For $f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-4}{x-2}$, which point is a removable-type singularity?
options: $x=-2$ only

questions.question: For $f(x)=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x-1}\right)$, which point is the natural singularity?
options: $x=\pi$

questions.question: Why does regular behaviour in a punctured neighbourhood matter for singularities?
options: It proves the function is continuous at $x_0$.
It makes every discontinuity removable.
It isolates a failure at $x_0$ from nearby irregularity.
It forces the function to be bounded.

questions.question: Suppose $f$ is continuous on $(-1,0)\cup(0,1)$ but is not defined at $0$. What conclusion follows?
options: $0$ cannot be a singularity because nearby behaviour is regular.
$0$ is a singularity of $f$.
$f$ must be continuous at $0$.
$f$ has no punctured neighbourhood around $0$.
